paper.title: Damage-induced reactive oxygen species regulate vimentin and dynamic collagen-based projections to mediate wound repair
paper.abstract: Tissue injury leads to early wound-associated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production that mediate tissue regeneration. To identify mechanisms that function downstream of redox signals that modulate regeneration, a vimentin reporter of mesenchymal cells was generated by driving GFP from the vimentin promoter in zebrafish. Early redox signaling mediated vimentin reporter activity at the wound margin. Moreover, both ROS and vimentin were necessary for collagen production and reorganization into projections at the leading edge of the wound. Second harmonic generation time-lapse imaging revealed that the collagen projections were associated with dynamic epithelial extensions at the wound edge during wound repair. Perturbing collagen organization by burn wound disrupted epithelial projections and subsequent wound healing. Taken together our findings suggest that ROS and vimentin integrate early wound signals to orchestrate the formation of collagen-based projections that guide regenerative growth during efficient wound repair.

nodes.label: Vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced ROS signaling to regulate collage…
nodes.claim: Vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced ROS signaling to regulate collagen expression and reorganization during zebrafish caudal fin regeneration, through a previously unknown mechanism whereby collagen projections at the wound edge guide epithelial growth.
nodes.verbatim_quote: In this study, we demonstrated that vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced redox signaling and regulates collagen expression and reorganization during wound repair. Using live imaging, our work uncovered a previously unknown mechanism whereby collagen projections at the wound edge guide epithelial growth during fin regeneration, a process dependent on vimentin.

strengths: The paper provides multiple independent lines of evidence connecting ROS → vimentin → collagen → epithelial projections → regeneration, forming a coherent signaling chain.
Both genetic (morpholino, CRISPR) and pharmacological approaches are used to perturb the pathway at multiple nodes.
Live imaging of SHG fibers and epithelial cell dynamics provides direct visual evidence of collagen-epithelial association during wound healing.
Prior work by Yoo et al. (2012) established the role of early ROS in fin regeneration, providing a validated foundation for the upstream part of this pathway.
The finding that vimentin regulates collagen accumulation is consistent with Cheng et al. (2016) and Eckes et al. (2000) in mouse wound models.
weaknesses: The claim that collagen projections 'guide' epithelial growth is based on correlative imaging data; no direct causal manipulation of collagen projections independent of vimentin or ROS is presented. The burn model and BAPN experiments are confounded by widespread tissue damage and toxicity, respectively.

The NFκB component of the pathway relies heavily on Withaferin A, which the authors themselves acknowledge can directly inhibit vimentin protein, creating a confound that undermines the specificity of NFκB as the mediator.
The mechanism by which vimentin-positive cells (which appear non-migratory and non-epithelial) regulate collagen expression/organization in adjacent tissues remains entirely unclear.

Many experiments rely on morpholino knockdown, which is known to produce off-target effects. While CRISPR F0 mosaics are used as partial confirmation, stable mutant lines were not generated or analyzed.

Sample sizes for some key quantifications (e.g., n=12 fins for DPI vim:egfp intensity; n=3 replicate percentages for projection scoring) are modest, and the projection scoring appears somewhat subjective.

The 'previously unknown mechanism' language overstates the novelty given that the role of collagen scaffolds in guiding cell behavior during wound healing is well established in clinical and in vitro literature.
alternative_interpretations: The observed collagen projections may be a passive consequence of wound geometry and existing actinotrichia structure rather than an actively guided process. The epithelial cells could simply be wrapping around pre-existing structural elements exposed by transection.

ROS inhibition and vimentin depletion may impair regeneration through broader effects on proliferation, immune cell function, or other signaling pathways, with collagen changes being a secondary consequence rather than the primary mechanism.
The association between vimentin+ cells and collagen fibers could reflect a response to mechanical cues from the ECM rather than vimentin driving collagen organization.
required_assumptions: The Tg(−2vim:egfp) reporter faithfully reflects endogenous vimentin expression.
Morpholino and CRISPR F0 mosaic approaches achieve sufficient and specific knockdown.
SHG signal changes reflect biologically meaningful alterations in collagen organization rather than imaging artifacts.
The pathway is linear (ROS → NFκB → vimentin → collagen → projections → regeneration) rather than involving parallel or feedback mechanisms.
Observations in zebrafish larval fin are relevant to wound healing mechanisms more broadly.
evaluation.notes: This is an ambitious root claim integrating multiple experimental observations. While each individual link in the chain has some evidence, the overall pathway is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The 'guidance' mechanism is the weakest link, relying on correlative imaging rather than direct manipulation of collagen projections.

nodes.label: The Tg(−2vim:egfp) reporter line faithfully recapitulates vimentin expression pa…
nodes.claim: The Tg(−2vim:egfp) reporter line faithfully recapitulates vimentin expression patterns and provides a powerful tool to report vimentin promoter activity and mesenchymal cell identity in larval zebrafish.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Taken together, these data show that the Tg(−2vim:egfp) line recapitulated previously published in situ vimentin expression data and vimentin was expressed in cells undergoing EMT, thereby providing a powerful tool to report vimentin promoter activity in larval zebrafish.

strengths: Expression pattern matches published in situ hybridization data from Cerdà et al. (1998), providing validation of spatial fidelity.
The EMT responsiveness (HRasV12 vs HRasG12) provides functional validation that the reporter reflects a biologically meaningful vimentin-associated process.
Multiple tissues and developmental stages were examined.
weaknesses: Only 2 kb of promoter region was used, which may not capture all regulatory elements; enhancers or silencers outside this region could mean the reporter misses or gains expression in certain contexts.
The EMT experiment was observed in only two replicates, with no quantification provided.
No direct comparison between endogenous vimentin protein expression and EGFP reporter activity was performed (e.g., co-staining with anti-vimentin antibody).
The claim that this is a 'powerful tool' for reporting mesenchymal cell identity is strong given that the reporter has not been validated against other mesenchymal markers.
GFP protein stability/turnover differs from endogenous vimentin, which could create temporal artifacts in expression reporting.
alternative_interpretations: The reporter may label only a subset of vimentin-expressing cells or may label some cells that don't express endogenous vimentin, due to incomplete promoter recapitulation.
required_assumptions: 2 kb upstream region contains sufficient regulatory elements for faithful vimentin expression.
EGFP maturation and degradation kinetics do not significantly distort the temporal pattern of vimentin expression.
Published in situ hybridization data is itself accurate and comprehensive.
evaluation.notes: The reporter is a useful tool but its characterization is incomplete. The lack of protein-level validation (anti-vimentin antibody co-staining) is a notable gap for a claim about faithfulness of reporter activity.

nodes.label: Wounding induces a population of non-migratory vimentin-positive cells at the wo…
nodes.claim: Wounding induces a population of non-migratory vimentin-positive cells at the wound edge, and this induction is regulated by early ROS signaling, likely through NFκB activity.
nodes.verbatim_quote: However, the findings suggest that early ROS signaling, likely at least in part through NFκB activity, regulates vimentin promoter activation at 1 dpw following caudal fin amputation.

strengths: Both in situ hybridization and live reporter imaging confirm wound-induced vimentin expression at the wound edge.
Time-lapse imaging directly demonstrates non-migratory behavior of vim+ cells.
Both pharmacological (DPI) and genetic (Duox1 MO) ROS inhibition reduce vimentin expression, providing convergent evidence.
The ROS-NFκB connection is supported by prior work showing DUOX1-dependent NFκB activation after fin amputation (de Oliveira et al., 2014).
weaknesses: The 'non-migratory' claim is based on time-lapse imaging resolution (~12-25 min intervals), which may miss rapid migration followed by arrest.
The identity of the cells that turn on vimentin remains unknown—the authors cannot identify whether these are resident fibroblasts, progenitors, or other cell types.
The NFκB link relies solely on Withaferin A, which has pleiotropic effects including direct vimentin inhibition, as acknowledged by the authors. No genetic NFκB perturbation was used.
The quantification of vim:egfp intensity (n=12 fins, p=0.0282) is relatively weak statistically and the sample size is modest.
The phrase 'likely through NFκB activity' is speculative given the tool limitations.
alternative_interpretations: The vim+ cells could be pre-existing mesenchymal cells that upregulate vimentin in response to local wound signals (e.g., cytokines, mechanical stress) rather than through a specific ROS→NFκB pathway.
DPI has known off-target effects beyond NADPH oxidase inhibition (including mitochondrial complex I), so ROS-independent effects could contribute.
Cells could migrate to the wound edge before imaging begins (prior to 12 hpw) and then become non-motile.
required_assumptions: DPI specifically inhibits wound-induced ROS without significant off-target effects at the doses used.
The temporal resolution of time-lapse imaging is sufficient to definitively characterize cell migration behavior.
Withaferin A effects on vimentin promoter activation reflect NFκB inhibition rather than direct vimentin effects.
evaluation.notes: The non-migratory nature of vim+ cells is an interesting observation but not definitively established. The NFκB link is the weakest component due to tool limitations.

nodes.label: Vimentin is required for efficient caudal fin regeneration in zebrafish larvae, …
nodes.claim: Vimentin is required for efficient caudal fin regeneration in zebrafish larvae, consistent with wound healing defects in vimentin-null mice.
nodes.verbatim_quote: In accordance with previous studies in other species, these data show that vimentin is required for efficient wound healing.

strengths: Multiple independent approaches converge: MO1, MO2, CRISPR F0 mosaics all show regeneration defects.
RNA rescue of MO1 confirms specificity of the morpholino effect.
Wound-specificity is demonstrated by lack of developmental fin defects in morphants.
TUNEL staining rules out gross cell survival differences as a confound.
Consistent with Eckes et al. (2000) and Cheng et al. (2016) who showed wound healing defects in vimentin-null mice.
Large sample sizes (n=85 per treatment for MO; n=119-130 for CRISPR) with high statistical significance (p<0.0001).
weaknesses: CRISPR F0 mosaics have variable mutational efficiency across cells and animals; stable homozygous mutant lines would be more definitive.
The CRISPR validation by sequencing shows only a 7 bp deletion in one example; the extent of mosaicism and proportion of null alleles across the F0 population is not systematically quantified.
The F0 CRISPR mutants showed a slight increase in developmental fin area (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G), which complicates interpretation.
Morpholinos can have off-target effects and their efficacy decreases with time; knockdown at 3 dpw may be incomplete.
alternative_interpretations: Vimentin depletion could affect regeneration through effects on immune cell function, blastema formation, or other processes not examined, rather than specifically through collagen/projection mechanisms.
required_assumptions: Morpholino knockdown persists sufficiently through the 3 dpw assessment period.
CRISPR F0 mosaics have sufficient penetrance of null alleles to produce a meaningful phenotype.
The regeneration defect reflects a specific wound healing mechanism rather than general cellular dysfunction.
evaluation.notes: This is one of the best-supported claims in the paper, with multiple convergent approaches and appropriate controls. The main caveat is the lack of stable mutant lines.

nodes.label: Regenerative wound healing involves the formation of epithelial projections at t…
nodes.claim: Regenerative wound healing involves the formation of epithelial projections at the wound edge — a novel feature not present during normal development — and vimentin is required for the formation of these projections.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The formation of these epithelial extensions, herein referred to as projections, was not present during normal development of the caudal fin, which occurred with the extension of a smooth fin edge.

strengths: Time-lapse imaging provides direct visualization of projection formation during wound healing.
The distinction between wound-induced projections and smooth developmental growth is clearly demonstrated.
Multiple perturbations (vimentin MO, DPI, WA) all reduce projection formation, providing convergent evidence.
Quantification of projection frequency is performed across replicates.
weaknesses: The scoring of 'visible projections' appears subjective; the criteria for what constitutes a projection are not rigorously defined, and no blinding is mentioned for the scoring.
The vimentin MO result shows 40% of morphants still form projections, suggesting the effect is partial and other mechanisms contribute.
The 95% CI for vim MO projection percentage (7.56% to 65.78%) is extremely wide, indicating high variability and low precision.
The claim that projections are 'novel' and 'previously unknown' is not substantiated with a systematic literature search.
Statistical analysis uses n=3 replicate percentages rather than individual larvae as the unit of analysis, reducing power.
No quantitative characterization of projection morphology (length, width, number) is provided.
alternative_interpretations: The 'projections' could be a normal variation in wound edge morphology that is suppressed by the global effects of vimentin depletion or ROS inhibition on cell health/proliferation rather than a specific vimentin-dependent mechanism.
The smooth edge in vim-deficient larvae could reflect delayed wound closure rather than a fundamentally different mode of healing.
required_assumptions: Visual scoring of projections is reliable and reproducible.
Projections are functionally important for regeneration rather than an epiphenomenon.
The absence of projections during normal development indicates they are wound-specific rather than being below detection threshold.
evaluation.notes: The projection phenotype is interesting but the quantification is weak. The wide confidence intervals and subjective scoring approach limit confidence in the magnitude of the effect.

nodes.label: Collagen fiber projections physically guide epithelial cell extensions at the wo…
nodes.claim: Collagen fiber projections physically guide epithelial cell extensions at the wound edge, pushing the healing plane forward during fin regeneration.
nodes.verbatim_quote: These findings suggest that the SHG fibers in the caudal fin, which we have previously shown are important for proper wound healing, play a guidance role in the formation of epithelial projections during wound repair.

strengths: Multiple imaging modalities (bright field, LC-PolScope, SHG, fluorescence) consistently show collagen fibers within epithelial projections.
Live dual imaging of SHG and Tg(krt4:egfp-caax) provides dynamic evidence of the fiber-epithelium association.
The observation of stretched cell membranes around fibers suggests physical interaction rather than mere co-localization.
Time-lapse videos show temporal correlation between fiber extension and epithelial progression.
weaknesses: The claim that fibers 'physically guide' or 'push' epithelial cells is an interpretation of imaging data; no direct test of mechanical causation is performed (e.g., laser ablation of individual fibers to test if epithelial progression halts).
Correlation between fiber and cell extension does not establish that fibers drive the process; epithelial cells could actively migrate and fibers could be passively pushed or deposited.
The temporal resolution of imaging (~15 min intervals) may be insufficient to determine which extends first—the fiber or the cell.
No measurement of forces (e.g., traction force microscopy) is provided to support the 'pushing' interpretation.
The term 'guide' implies directionality and causation that goes beyond what the imaging data can demonstrate.
alternative_interpretations: Epithelial cells could be actively migrating and depositing or reorganizing collagen as they go, rather than being pushed by collagen.
The projections could be driven by localized proliferation at the wound edge, with collagen fibers simply being incorporated into the growing tissue.
Both fiber extension and cell projection could be independently driven by a common upstream signal (e.g., growth factors) rather than one guiding the other.
required_assumptions: The temporal association observed in live imaging reflects a causal relationship (fiber extension causes cell progression).
SHG signal accurately represents collagen fiber structure and not other birefringent materials.
The 'stretching' of cell membranes around fibers reflects physical stress rather than active cell remodeling.
evaluation.notes: This is the most mechanistically novel claim in the paper but also the least rigorously demonstrated. The imaging is beautiful and suggestive but does not establish causation. Direct manipulation experiments (e.g., laser ablation of individual collagen fibers) would be needed.

nodes.label: Vimentin regulates wound-induced collagen expression and the dynamic reorganizat…
nodes.claim: Vimentin regulates wound-induced collagen expression and the dynamic reorganization of collagen fibers at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: we support, and extend, the evidence of these previous studies by showing a critical role for vimentin in both collagen expression and its dynamic reorganization during the repair process in zebrafish larvae.

strengths: qRT-PCR demonstrates reduced col1a1 and col2a1b expression in vimentin-depleted larvae with statistically significant results.
SHG imaging quantification shows both reduced contour length and altered fiber angle in vim MO larvae.
The collagen expression regulation is consistent with in vitro data from Challa and Stefanovic (2011) showing vimentin-Larp6 regulation of collagen I mRNA.
Multiple perturbations (vim MO, DPI, WA) all show convergent effects on collagen expression and fiber organization.
CurveAlign analysis provides quantitative, unbiased assessment of fiber orientation.
weaknesses: The mechanism by which vimentin (in mesenchymal cells) regulates collagen expression (measured from the whole fin tip including epithelial cells) is not elucidated. Is it cell-autonomous or paracrine?
qRT-PCR measures bulk tissue RNA from a heterogeneous cell population; cell-type-specific collagen regulation cannot be determined.

The connection between collagen expression changes and fiber organization changes is assumed but not directly demonstrated; reduced expression could simply mean less collagen rather than disorganized collagen.
The Larp6 data (Figure 6—supplement) shows only a partial phenocopy (area but not length defect), suggesting the mechanism is more complex than presented.
The collagen II labeling at broken SHG fiber tips is noted but not investigated, leaving a potentially important observation unexplored.
alternative_interpretations: Vimentin depletion could reduce the number of fibroblasts at the wound (as in Eckes et al., 2000 mouse model), leading to reduced collagen production as a secondary consequence rather than a direct regulatory mechanism.
The SHG fiber disorganization could reflect general tissue disorganization from impaired wound healing rather than a specific effect on collagen organization.
required_assumptions: qRT-PCR from the fin tip region accurately reflects wound-specific collagen expression changes.
SHG signal changes reflect collagen organization rather than other fibrillar matrix changes.
The vimentin-Larp6-collagen I pathway described in vitro operates similarly in vivo in zebrafish.
evaluation.notes: The evidence for reduced collagen expression is solid; the evidence for vimentin directly controlling collagen reorganization (as opposed to simply affecting collagen levels, which then affects organization) is less clear.

nodes.label: Direct disruption of collagen organization — through inhibition of cross-linking…
nodes.claim: Direct disruption of collagen organization — through inhibition of cross-linking or destruction of fibers by thermal injury — impairs epithelial projection formation and subsequent wound healing.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Treatments that disrupt collagen organization, such as inhibition of cross-linking or destruction of collagen fibers by thermal injury, diminished the formation of epithelial projections and subsequent wound healing was impaired.

strengths: Two independent approaches (BAPN and burn) both disrupt collagen and impair healing, providing convergent evidence.
The burn model provides a dramatically different collagen phenotype (complete loss near wound) that is informative.
The burn wound experiment shows a clear correlation between loss of SHG fibers, loss of projections, and impaired healing.
Statistical significance is achieved for both projection frequency and healing area comparisons.
weaknesses: BAPN causes lethality between 4-5 dpf, as acknowledged by the authors, making it impossible to separate toxic effects from specific collagen cross-linking effects. The authors note 'it is possible that the observed effects on regeneration were in part due to toxicity.'

The burn wound causes extensive tissue damage beyond just collagen destruction—thermal injury damages cells, denatures proteins, disrupts vasculature, and triggers different inflammatory responses. The healing defect cannot be attributed specifically to collagen loss.
Comparing burn wounds to amputation wounds is problematic because these are fundamentally different types of injuries with different damage patterns, inflammatory responses, and healing dynamics.
The BAPN contour length actually increased rather than decreased, which contradicts the overall narrative; the authors explain this away but it creates inconsistency.
No rescue experiment is performed (e.g., providing exogenous collagen scaffold after burn to restore healing).
alternative_interpretations: Burn wound healing may be impaired due to extensive cell death and protein denaturation rather than specifically due to collagen fiber loss.
BAPN toxicity, rather than specific inhibition of collagen cross-linking, could be responsible for the healing defect.
The impaired healing could reflect damage to non-collagenous ECM components, signaling molecules, or cell populations.
required_assumptions: BAPN effects are primarily through collagen cross-linking inhibition rather than generalized toxicity.
Burn wound effects on healing are primarily mediated through collagen fiber destruction rather than other forms of thermal damage.
Comparing amputation and burn wounds is a valid experimental design for isolating the contribution of collagen fibers.
evaluation.notes: This is the weakest primary claim. Both perturbations (BAPN and burn) have major confounds that prevent attribution of the healing defect specifically to collagen disruption. The claim would be much stronger with more specific interventions (e.g., collagenase treatment, or laser ablation of individual fibers).

nodes.label: The reporter line shows EGFP expression in cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord n…
nodes.claim: The reporter line shows EGFP expression in cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord neurons, the opercle, and fin mesenchymal cells, consistent with published in situ hybridization data.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This expression pattern is consistent with the vimentin expression pattern previously shown by in situ hybridization.

strengths: The expression pattern in cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord neurons, and opercle matches Cerdà et al. (1998) in situ data.
Multiple developmental stages are shown (two somite through 4 dpf).
Expression in fin mesenchymal cells at 3 dpf is also documented.
weaknesses: The comparison to published in situ data is qualitative, not quantitative.
No co-staining with anti-vimentin antibody is performed to verify protein-level correspondence.
The absence of EGFP in any tissue that should express vimentin would be difficult to detect without systematic comparison.
required_assumptions: Published in situ hybridization data from Cerdà et al. (1998) is comprehensive and accurate.
Visual comparison of expression patterns is sufficient to claim consistency.
evaluation.notes: Descriptive data that is straightforward but would benefit from more rigorous validation.

nodes.label: The reporter responds to EMT induction, as oncogenic HRasV12 but not wild-type H…
nodes.claim: The reporter responds to EMT induction, as oncogenic HRasV12 but not wild-type HRasG12 induces vimentin promoter activity.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Overexpression of oncogenic HRasV12, but not wild type HRasG12, induced vimentin promoter activity and expression of EGFP that co-localized in the same cells expressing HRasV12.

strengths: The EMT induction paradigm (oncogenic Ras) is well-established from Freisinger and Huttenlocher (2014).
Co-localization of EGFP and RFP in HRasV12-expressing cells is a compelling demonstration of cell-autonomous reporter activation.
The negative control (HRasG12) strengthens the specificity of the finding.
weaknesses: Only two replicates were performed for this experiment.
No quantification of co-localization efficiency or penetrance is provided.
Transient mosaic expression means only a subset of cells express the construct, limiting the generalizability.
The EMT responsiveness validates one aspect of vimentin biology but does not fully validate the reporter for wound healing contexts.
alternative_interpretations: The reporter could respond to oncogenic stress signaling rather than specifically to EMT.
required_assumptions: Oncogenic Ras-driven EGFP induction reflects genuine EMT-associated vimentin expression rather than non-specific promoter activation.
Two replicates are sufficient for this qualitative observation.
evaluation.notes: Suggestive but underpowered experiment. The qualitative observation is compelling but lacks rigor for definitive claims.

nodes.label: Tail transection induces localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 h…
nodes.claim: Tail transection induces localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hours post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: tail transection induced localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hr post wound (hpw), an outcome not observed with the sense probe.

strengths: Both whole mount in situ hybridization and live reporter imaging confirm wound-induced vimentin at the wound edge.
Sense probe control rules out non-specific in situ signal.
Time course from live imaging (no signal at 2 hpw, signal at 20 hpw, enhanced at 26 hpw) shows temporal dynamics.
Two independent methods (ISH and transgenic reporter) converge on the same conclusion.
weaknesses: In situ hybridization experiments were only observed in two experiments.
No quantification of in situ signal intensity is provided.
Only 24 hpw timepoint shown for ISH; earlier timepoints would better define onset.
required_assumptions: The wound edge signal is newly induced rather than residual from pre-existing vim+ cells that survived amputation.
evaluation.notes: Solid evidence from two independent methods.

nodes.label: The vim+ cells at the wound do not migrate from surrounding tissue but rather ar…
nodes.claim: The vim+ cells at the wound do not migrate from surrounding tissue but rather arise as a non-motile population of cells that activate the vimentin promoter at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Surprisingly, the vim+ cells did not migrate to the wound from surrounding fin tissue but rather expression developed in what appeared to be a non-motile population of cells at the wound edge.

strengths: Time-lapse imaging directly tracks cell behavior over time, which is the appropriate method for this claim.
The observation is consistent across the time-lapse videos presented.
weaknesses: Imaging begins at 12 hpw, so cells could have migrated to the wound edge before imaging started.
The temporal resolution (~12-25 min intervals) could miss rapid migration events.
The authors themselves acknowledge they cannot exclude that 'a specialized population of cells migrates to the wound edge and subsequently activates the vimentin promoter.'
No cell tracking quantification (speed, displacement) is provided to support the 'non-motile' claim.
EGFP maturation time (which can be hours) means that cells could have migrated before becoming fluorescent.
alternative_interpretations: Cells could migrate to the wound edge during the 0-12 hpw window before imaging begins, then become non-motile and turn on vimentin.
The apparent in situ activation could reflect EGFP maturation kinetics rather than promoter activation timing.
required_assumptions: Imaging from 12 hpw captures the relevant period of potential cell migration.
EGFP maturation time does not create a significant lag that obscures migration.
The temporal resolution is sufficient to detect migratory behavior.
evaluation.notes: The non-migratory claim is intriguing but has significant technical limitations that prevent definitive conclusions. See c1.2.3 for related identity issues.

nodes.label: The wound-induced vim+ cells do not appear to derive from epithelial cells, macr…
nodes.claim: The wound-induced vim+ cells do not appear to derive from epithelial cells, macrophages, or leukocytes, though the authors cannot exclude their origin from a progenitor population.
nodes.verbatim_quote: It is possible that a specialized population of cells, including a type of progenitor cell, migrates to the wound edge from the surrounding tissue and subsequently activates the vimentin promoter, although our studies cannot confirm this possibility.

strengths: Multiple exclusion experiments are performed: krt4 co-localization, macrophage marker, pu.1 MO depletion.
The authors are appropriately cautious, noting they 'cannot confirm' the progenitor possibility.
weaknesses: The identity of the vim+ cells remains completely unresolved, which is a major gap.
Only one macrophage marker (mpeg1:dendra2) is used; this does not exclude other immune cell types or tissue-resident macrophage subsets.
The pu.1 MO depletes all leukocytes, which is a broad manipulation that affects multiple cell types and could have compensatory effects.
No positive identification markers were tested (fibroblast markers, progenitor markers, etc.).
The statement 'did not appear to arise from epithelial cells based on live imaging' relies on the same temporal resolution limitations discussed for c1.2.2.
alternative_interpretations: The vim+ cells could be fibroblasts that are already present in the tissue but below detection threshold for the reporter until wound signals upregulate vimentin.
They could be perivascular cells, neural crest-derived cells, or other mesenchymal populations.
required_assumptions: The markers used (krt4, mpeg1) are comprehensive enough to exclude the respective cell types.
The pu.1 MO is effective at depleting the relevant leukocyte populations.
evaluation.notes: The negative data (ruling out certain cell types) is useful but the lack of positive identification leaves the cell identity question unresolved, which weakens the mechanistic interpretations throughout the paper.

nodes.label: Early ROS inhibition (pharmacological or genetic) is sufficient to impair viment…
nodes.claim: Early ROS inhibition (pharmacological or genetic) is sufficient to impair vimentin promoter activation at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: inhibition of ROS for 1 hr before and 1 hr after wounding was sufficient to impair the appearance of vim+ cells at the wound edge 1 dpw in the Tg(−2vim:egfp) line.

strengths: Both pharmacological (DPI) and genetic (Duox1 MO) approaches show the same result.
The brief treatment window (1 hr pre- and post-wounding) demonstrates that early ROS specifically is sufficient.
Quantification by fluorescence intensity ratio provides objective measurement.
Consistent with Yoo et al. (2012) who established the importance of early ROS for fin regeneration.
weaknesses: The sample size is modest (n=12 total fins over three replicates, with 2 to 6 fins per treatment per replicate).
DPI is not specific to NADPH oxidases and can inhibit other flavin-containing enzymes including mitochondrial complex I and nitric oxide synthase.
The Duox1 MO result is described qualitatively ('similar results were observed') without quantification shown in the main figures.
The p-value (0.0282) is statistically significant but not robust, particularly given the small sample size and multiple comparisons context.
alternative_interpretations: DPI could impair vimentin expression through effects on cellular metabolism or mitochondrial function rather than specifically through ROS.
Early ROS could be required for general wound signaling (inflammation, immune cell recruitment) which then secondarily affects vimentin expression.
required_assumptions: DPI treatment window is specific enough to target wound-induced ROS rather than baseline redox signaling.
Fluorescence intensity ratio is a valid quantification approach for reporter activity.
evaluation.notes: The convergence of pharmacological and genetic approaches strengthens this claim, but the small sample sizes and known DPI off-target effects are concerning.

nodes.label: NFκB inhibition blocks vimentin promoter activation at the wound, though the pha…
nodes.claim: NFκB inhibition blocks vimentin promoter activation at the wound, though the pharmacological inhibitor used (Withaferin A) can also directly inhibit vimentin protein.
nodes.verbatim_quote: It should be noted that WA can directly inhibit the vimentin protein, and thus the influence of WA downstream of vimentin promoter activation must also be considered.

strengths: The result is consistent with the known role of NFκB as a redox-sensitive transcription factor.
Previous work by de Oliveira et al. (2014) showed DUOX1-dependent NFκB activation after fin amputation, providing biological plausibility.
weaknesses: The authors themselves acknowledge that Withaferin A 'can directly inhibit the vimentin protein,' making it impossible to distinguish NFκB-mediated effects on the vimentin promoter from direct effects on vimentin protein stability/function.
No genetic NFκB perturbation (e.g., IκB super-repressor, p65 knockdown) is used to validate the WA result.
Only one pharmacological tool is used for NFκB, with no dose-response data.
No measurement of NFκB activity (e.g., using the Tg(nfκb:egfp) line) is performed in parallel with vimentin reporter assessment to confirm NFκB is actually inhibited.
alternative_interpretations: WA could block vimentin reporter signal by directly destabilizing vimentin protein (and thus any vimentin-positive feedback) rather than through NFκB inhibition.
WA has additional targets beyond NFκB and vimentin, including effects on proteasome activity and NF-κB-independent anti-inflammatory pathways.
required_assumptions: WA primarily works through NFκB inhibition at the doses used.
The direct vimentin-binding activity of WA does not confound interpretation of promoter-level effects.
evaluation.notes: The NFκB link is the most speculative part of the signaling pathway. The dual activity of WA makes this claim essentially untestable with this single tool.

nodes.label: Vim+ cells are tightly associated with SHG collagen fibers in the fin, and their…
nodes.claim: Vim+ cells are tightly associated with SHG collagen fibers in the fin, and their morphology correlates with fiber alignment status.
nodes.verbatim_quote: In wounded caudal fins we observed vim+ cells with a more rounded morphology in regions of the fin characterized by mis-aligned SHG collagen fibers and the elongated cells in regions of the fin with intact collagen fibers.

strengths: SHG imaging combined with the vim:egfp reporter provides direct visualization of the spatial relationship.
3D reconstruction confirms the association is not an artifact of 2D projection.
The morphological correlation (elongated cells on aligned fibers, rounded cells near misaligned fibers) suggests functional interaction.
Both unwounded and wounded conditions are examined.
weaknesses: The association is correlative; it does not establish that vim+ cells regulate fiber alignment or vice versa.
No quantification of the co-localization or morphological categories is provided.
Only two replicates (24 live larvae) for the wounded condition.
alternative_interpretations: Vim+ cells may simply preferentially attach to collagen fibers as a substrate, with their morphology reflecting fiber orientation rather than any regulatory relationship.
Both cell morphology and fiber alignment could be independently determined by tissue architecture.
required_assumptions: The spatial association detected by imaging reflects a biologically meaningful relationship.
Cell morphology changes reflect functional state rather than fixation or imaging artifacts.
evaluation.notes: Descriptive but compelling imaging data. The morphological correlation is interesting and supports the overall narrative.

nodes.label: Morpholino depletion of vimentin impairs regenerate area and length at 3 dpw.
nodes.claim: Morpholino depletion of vimentin impairs regenerate area and length at 3 dpw.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We found that vimentin-deficient larvae had impaired regenerate area and regenerate length at 3 dpw

strengths: Large sample size (n=85 per treatment over four replicates).
Highly significant result (p<0.0001).
Both area and length measurements show the same trend.
95% confidence intervals show clear separation between groups.
weaknesses: Morpholino efficacy may wane by 3 dpw (5-6 dpf), potentially underestimating the full effect.
No Western blot or protein-level quantification of vimentin knockdown efficiency is shown at the time of assessment.
required_assumptions: Morpholino knockdown persists through the assessment period.
The control morpholino does not itself affect regeneration.
evaluation.notes: Straightforward and well-powered result.

nodes.label: CRISPR-Cas9 mosaic F0 vimentin mutants also display reduced regeneration, confir…
nodes.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 mosaic F0 vimentin mutants also display reduced regeneration, confirming the morpholino result.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The mosaic F0 mutants also displayed reduced regenerate length and area at 3 dpw

strengths: Independent genetic approach confirms morpholino result.
Large sample sizes (n=119-130 over 3 replicates).
Highly significant (p<0.0001).
CRISPR validation includes sequencing of individual embryos and germline DNA.
weaknesses: F0 mosaic mutants have variable mutational burden across animals; the degree of vimentin loss in each larva is unknown.
Only one example of sequencing is shown (7 bp deletion); the spectrum and frequency of mutations across the population is not systematically characterized.
The slight increase in developmental fin area in CRISPR mutants (Figure 3—supplement 3G) is unexplained and could represent a confound.
Stable homozygous mutant lines would provide much stronger evidence.
alternative_interpretations: Variable mosaicism could mean the phenotype is driven by a subset of highly mutant animals, with many animals having minimal vimentin loss.
required_assumptions: F0 CRISPR mosaics achieve sufficient penetrance of disruptive mutations to meaningfully reduce vimentin.
The guide RNA is specific to vimentin without significant off-target cutting.
evaluation.notes: Valuable confirmatory data but F0 mosaics are inherently noisy. The statistical significance despite this noise is encouraging.

nodes.label: The regeneration defect is wound-specific and not attributable to developmental …
nodes.claim: The regeneration defect is wound-specific and not attributable to developmental effects on fin growth or changes in cell survival.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This defect was wound-specific, as unwounded morphants did not display a defect in fin length or area compared to age matched controls during normal development.

strengths: Developmental fin measurements in unwounded morphants show no defect, clearly demonstrating wound-specificity.
TUNEL staining at 1 hpw rules out gross apoptosis as a confound.
Multiple metrics (fin area and length) assessed for developmental controls.
weaknesses: TUNEL was only assessed at 1 hpw; cell death at later timepoints (relevant to the 3 dpw assessment) was not examined.
Developmental fin data represents a single experiment in duplicate (Figure 3—supplement 1G,H), which is limited.
Other potential developmental effects (cell proliferation, differentiation) are not examined.
alternative_interpretations: Vimentin depletion could specifically impair wound-associated proliferation (at timepoints not assessed by TUNEL) rather than the collagen/projection mechanism proposed.
required_assumptions: 1 hpw TUNEL is representative of cell survival throughout the regeneration period.
Absence of developmental fin defects means vimentin function is specifically wound-related.
evaluation.notes: The wound-specificity argument is sound for gross morphology but the single-timepoint TUNEL is limited.

nodes.label: The regeneration defect can be rescued by co-injection of zebrafish vimentin RNA…
nodes.claim: The regeneration defect can be rescued by co-injection of zebrafish vimentin RNA, and is reproducible with a second independent morpholino.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Co-injection was sufficient to rescue the regeneration defect observed in the morphants, suggesting that vimentin is required for fin regeneration in zebrafish.

strengths: RNA rescue of MO1 is the gold standard for confirming morpholino specificity.
A second independent morpholino (MO2) reproducing the phenotype further validates specificity.
Both area and length defects are rescued/reproduced.
weaknesses: The rescue data are pooled from only two replicates.
No quantification of rescue efficiency (how much vimentin protein is restored) is provided.
The second MO (MO2) validation is briefly presented without detailed characterization.
required_assumptions: Co-injected RNA produces functional vimentin protein at relevant levels.
The rescue is not due to non-specific effects of RNA injection.
evaluation.notes: The combination of rescue and second MO provides strong support for specificity.

nodes.label: Vimentin is not required for the activation of its own promoter at the wound edg…
nodes.claim: Vimentin is not required for the activation of its own promoter at the wound edge, indicating separable regulation of vimentin expression and vimentin function.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae displayed no defect in the appearance of vim+ cells at the wound edge following amputation, indicating that vimentin is not required for the activation of the vimentin promoter along the wound edge.

strengths: Clear demonstration that morpholino knockdown of vimentin protein does not prevent vimentin promoter activation, showing separable regulation.
Multiple timepoints (1, 2, 3 dpw) examined.
Logically consistent with MO targeting translation rather than transcription.
weaknesses: This is a qualitative observation from confocal images; no quantification of EGFP intensity is provided.

If the MO blocks translation, GFP translation should also theoretically be affected, unless the MO targets vimentin-specific UTR sequences not present in the reporter construct. This important technical detail is not discussed.
The observation could simply reflect the fact that the MO targets the endogenous vimentin mRNA but not the transgenic EGFP mRNA.
alternative_interpretations: The result may simply reflect the technical design of the MO (targeting endogenous vimentin mRNA) rather than revealing biology about separable regulation.
required_assumptions: The morpholino targets vimentin mRNA in a way that does not affect the transgenic reporter mRNA.
The reporter accurately reflects promoter activity independent of vimentin protein levels.
evaluation.notes: This is likely a technical observation based on MO design rather than a deep biological insight about separable regulation. The interpretation is overclaimed if the MO simply doesn't target the transgene.

nodes.label: Epithelial projections appear at the wound edge starting at 18 hpw and become pr…
nodes.claim: Epithelial projections appear at the wound edge starting at 18 hpw and become prominent by 24 hpw, but are absent during normal fin development.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The first visible projections after tail transection could be identified at 18 hpw and became prominent by 24 hpw.

strengths: Time-lapse microscopy directly demonstrates the temporal appearance of projections.
The comparison to developmental fin growth (smooth edge) is clearly shown.
Multiple time points documented (18, 24 hpw onward).
weaknesses: The developmental comparison (Figure 4—supplement 1A) is noted as a single experiment.
The definition of 'projection' remains somewhat subjective.
It is not clear whether the absence of projections during development reflects a different mechanism or simply slower growth dynamics.
alternative_interpretations: Projections during wound healing could reflect the uneven wound edge morphology from transection rather than a specific regenerative mechanism.
required_assumptions: The wound edge morphology is a biological response rather than an artifact of the transection procedure.
evaluation.notes: Descriptive observation that is clearly shown by imaging.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion dramatically reduces the proportion of larvae forming epithel…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion dramatically reduces the proportion of larvae forming epithelial projections.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae possessed a smooth wound edge and relative absence of the epithelial projections for more than 24 hpw.

strengths: The difference in projection frequency is statistically significant (p=0.0348).
Time-lapse video supports the qualitative observation of smooth wound edge in morphants.
weaknesses: The 95% CI for vim MO (7.56% to 65.78%) is extremely wide, indicating poor precision.
About 40% of morphants still form projections, suggesting the effect is incomplete and possibly confounded by variable MO efficacy.
Scoring of projections is binary (present/absent) and apparently subjective; no blinding is described.
The statistical analysis uses n=3 replicate percentages rather than individual animals.
alternative_interpretations: The partial effect could indicate that vimentin contributes to but is not essential for projection formation.
Variable MO knockdown efficiency across animals could explain why 40% still show projections.
required_assumptions: Binary projection scoring accurately captures the biological phenomenon.
The replicate-level statistical approach is appropriate for this type of data.
evaluation.notes: Statistically significant but imprecise result with high variability.

nodes.label: Early ROS inhibition and NFκB inhibition also impair epithelial projection forma…
nodes.claim: Early ROS inhibition and NFκB inhibition also impair epithelial projection formation.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Early pharmacological inhibition of ROS resulted in a smooth wound edge and impaired the formation of projections at 24 hpw.

strengths: DPI result is statistically significant (p=0.0129) and provides convergent evidence with vimentin depletion.
WA treatment shows similar effects.
Consistent with the proposed pathway (ROS → vimentin → projections).
weaknesses: Same subjective scoring and replicate-level statistics as c1.4.2.
DPI and WA have pleiotropic effects beyond the proposed pathway.
The DMSO 95% CI (31.76% to 99.58%) is extremely wide, indicating enormous variability in the control group.
With such wide CIs in both treatment groups, the biological significance of the difference is uncertain.
alternative_interpretations: ROS inhibition could impair projections through effects on cell proliferation, migration, or other signaling pathways independent of vimentin.
required_assumptions: The effects of DPI and WA on projections are mediated through the proposed pathway rather than through alternative mechanisms.
evaluation.notes: The convergence of multiple perturbations is a strength, but the wide confidence intervals in all experiments are concerning.

nodes.label: Fibrillar collagen structures are physically present within the epithelial proje…
nodes.claim: Fibrillar collagen structures are physically present within the epithelial projections and extend to their tips, appearing to induce physical stress on the epithelial cells.
nodes.verbatim_quote: These fibers appeared to induce a physical stress on the epithelial projections since the epithelial cells, whose membranes are also birefringent and can be detected with LC-PolScope microscopy, appear elongated, with the cell membranes stretched outward around the fiber.

strengths: Multiple imaging modalities converge: bright field, LC-PolScope, SHG, and phalloidin staining all identify fibrillar structures in projections.
LC-PolScope detection of birefringent fibers is consistent with collagen.
The observation of stretched cell membranes around fibers is clearly shown in the images.
Fixed and live imaging approaches are complementary.
weaknesses: The interpretation that fibers 'induce physical stress' on epithelial cells is an inference from static images (stretched membranes); no direct force measurement is performed.
The identity of the fibers as specifically collagen (versus elastin, actinotrichia, or other birefringent materials) is inferred but not definitively proven by LC-PolScope alone.
alternative_interpretations: The elongated cell morphology around fibers could reflect active cell migration along the fiber rather than passive stretching by the fiber.
required_assumptions: Birefringent fibers detected by LC-PolScope are collagen.
Elongated cell morphology reflects physical stress from fibers rather than active cell behavior.
evaluation.notes: The multi-modal imaging evidence for the physical presence of fibers in projections is compelling.

nodes.label: Live dual imaging of SHG fibers and epithelial cell membranes demonstrates that …
nodes.claim: Live dual imaging of SHG fibers and epithelial cell membranes demonstrates that extending SHG fibers push the healing plane forward.
nodes.verbatim_quote: 3D reconstruction surface rendering from time-lapse microscopy, collecting SHG and fluorescence signals in the Tg(krt4:egfp-caax) line, showed extending SHG fibers pushing the healing plane forward.

strengths: Live dual imaging is technically impressive and provides temporal information about the fiber-cell relationship.
3D surface rendering helps visualize the spatial relationship.
The time-lapse shows clear co-extension of fibers and cells.
weaknesses: The claim that fibers 'push' cells is an interpretation; the imaging cannot distinguish pushing from cells actively migrating along fibers.
No quantitative analysis of the relative timing (which extends first) is provided.
Temporal resolution (~15 min intervals) may not capture rapid dynamics.
This is essentially a single representative experiment; no quantification across multiple larvae is shown.
alternative_interpretations: Cells could be actively extending along pre-existing or newly deposited collagen, with the fibers serving as a substrate rather than a driving force.
Both fibers and cells could be driven forward by underlying tissue growth/proliferation.
required_assumptions: The 'pushing' interpretation is supported by the imaging data.
Representative videos reflect the general process.
evaluation.notes: The live imaging is technically excellent but the mechanistic interpretation (pushing vs. guiding vs. substrate) cannot be resolved by imaging alone.

nodes.label: This is claimed to be the first time collagen structure (SHG) and epithelial cel…
nodes.claim: This is claimed to be the first time collagen structure (SHG) and epithelial cell membranes were imaged long-term in vivo, enabling identification of these dynamic projections.
nodes.verbatim_quote: To our knowledge, this was the first time that collagen structure using SHG and epithelial cell membranes were imaged long term in vivo, allowing the identification of these dynamic cell projections that occur during fin growth after injury.

strengths: The technical achievement of long-term live SHG and fluorescence imaging in zebrafish larvae is genuinely impressive.
The authors appropriately qualify the claim with 'to our knowledge.'
weaknesses: Priority claims are difficult to verify and risky; other groups may have performed similar imaging without the authors' knowledge.
This is a claim about technical precedent rather than a scientific finding.
The novelty of the observation (projections) depends on this imaging capability, but the mechanism of the projections remains unclear.
required_assumptions: The authors have conducted a thorough literature search.
No comparable long-term in vivo SHG + fluorescence imaging has been published.
evaluation.notes: A technical achievement claim that is difficult to evaluate as a scientific claim.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion reduces SHG fiber projections (contour length) at the wound e…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion reduces SHG fiber projections (contour length) at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The vimentin-deficient larvae had a reduced contour length at the wound edges as compared to control larvae

strengths: Quantitative measurement of contour length provides an objective metric.
Good sample sizes (n=33 control, n=32 vim MO over 4 replicates).
Highly significant result (p=0.0009).
Supported by 3D reconstructions and videos.
weaknesses: Contour length is an indirect measure of fiber projections; shorter contour could reflect less tissue growth overall rather than specifically fewer projections.
The measurement is made from a specific region (posterior to notochord), which may not be representative of the entire wound.
alternative_interpretations: Reduced contour could simply reflect less overall regrowth rather than specifically fewer fiber projections.
required_assumptions: Contour length is a valid proxy for fiber projection formation.
The analyzed region is representative.
evaluation.notes: Well-quantified result with appropriate sample sizes.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion alters SHG fiber orientation, making fibers more parallel rat…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion alters SHG fiber orientation, making fibers more parallel rather than perpendicular to the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This analysis revealed that the population of fibers with vimentin depletion tended to be less perpendicular overall than their control counterparts.

strengths: CurveAlign is an established, unbiased quantification tool for fiber orientation analysis.
Good sample sizes (n=30-32 per group over 4 replicates).
Highly significant result (p=0.0003).
The analysis is well-described methodologically.
weaknesses: The biological significance of the mean angle difference (66-71° for control vs. 59-64° for vim MO) is modest in absolute terms.
The analysis measures all fibers within 60 microns of the wound edge, which may include fibers not involved in active reorganization.
Whether this angle change is causally related to impaired healing or is a consequence of generally impaired regeneration is unclear.
alternative_interpretations: The more parallel fiber orientation could be a consequence of reduced overall regrowth rather than a cause of it.
required_assumptions: Fiber angle relative to wound edge is a meaningful metric for fiber organization during healing.
The 60-micron window captures the relevant region of active reorganization.
evaluation.notes: Rigorous quantification with appropriate tools. The causal direction is uncertain.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion reduces wound-induced expression of col1a1 and col2a1b at 24 …
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion reduces wound-induced expression of col1a1 and col2a1b at 24 hpw.
nodes.verbatim_quote: At 24 hpw, vimentin-deficient larvae displayed a reduction in col1a1 and col2a1b expression at 24 hpw compared to controls.

strengths: qRT-PCR provides quantitative measurement of gene expression changes.
Both col1a1 (p=0.004, n=6) and col2a1b (p=0.0404, n=5) show significant reduction.
Consistent with Challa and Stefanovic (2011) who showed vimentin regulates collagen I mRNA stability in vitro.
The tissue collection method (fin tip ~500 µm) provides wound-relevant tissue.
weaknesses: qRT-PCR from heterogeneous tissue cannot determine which cell types show reduced collagen expression.
The reduction could be an indirect effect of fewer mesenchymal cells at the wound rather than direct transcriptional regulation.
The col2a1b p-value (0.0404) is marginal.
No protein-level assessment of collagen is provided (e.g., hydroxyproline assay).
alternative_interpretations: Reduced collagen expression could reflect fewer fibroblasts at the wound (as in Eckes et al., 2000 vimentin-null mice) rather than direct vimentin regulation of collagen transcription.
required_assumptions: RNA changes reflect biologically meaningful changes in collagen protein production.
The fin tip collection captures the relevant wound tissue without excessive dilution.
evaluation.notes: Solid qRT-PCR data, though the mechanism (direct vs. indirect) remains ambiguous.

nodes.label: Early ROS inhibition also reduces collagen expression and SHG fiber organization…
nodes.claim: Early ROS inhibition also reduces collagen expression and SHG fiber organization at the wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: pharmacological inhibition of early ROS signaling was sufficient to cause a significant reduction in the rise of collagen expression following amputation at 24 hpw.

strengths: DPI treatment shows significant reduction in both collagens, consistent with the proposed ROS → vimentin → collagen pathway.
WA treatment shows similar effects.
SHG contour length reduction is also shown.
weaknesses: DPI has known off-target effects beyond NADPH oxidase inhibition.
col1a1 p-value (0.0464) is marginal with n=4 replicates.
DPI could affect collagen expression through multiple mechanisms independent of vimentin.
The WA result has the same confound as discussed in c1.2.5.
alternative_interpretations: ROS inhibition could directly affect fibroblast function and collagen production independent of vimentin.
Metabolic effects of DPI could globally reduce biosynthetic capacity.
required_assumptions: DPI effects on collagen are mediated through the ROS → vimentin pathway.
evaluation.notes: Consistent with the model but does not definitively place collagen changes downstream of vimentin vs. as a parallel ROS-dependent event.

nodes.label: The SHG fibers in the caudal fin are composed of multiple collagen types, with b…
nodes.claim: The SHG fibers in the caudal fin are composed of multiple collagen types, with both SHG (type I/III) and type II collagen co-associating in projections.
nodes.verbatim_quote: both SHG fibers and Col II labeling still associated in projections and disrupted fibers.

strengths: Dual SHG and immunofluorescence provides direct visualization of co-localization.
Both unwounded and wounded conditions show co-association.
The observation of Col II caps at broken SHG fiber tips is novel and interesting.
Consistent with published composition of actinotrichia (Durán et al., 2011).
weaknesses: Only observed in two experiments.
No quantification of co-localization is provided.
The functional significance of Col II caps at broken fiber tips is not investigated.
required_assumptions: SHG signal represents type I/III collagen.
The Col II antibody is specific in zebrafish tissue.
evaluation.notes: Solid descriptive data with limited replication.

nodes.label: Vimentin regulation of col1a1 expression is mediated at least partly through Lar…
nodes.claim: Vimentin regulation of col1a1 expression is mediated at least partly through Larp6, suggesting vimentin influences wound healing through multiple pathways.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Larp6-deficient larvae displayed a significant defect in regenerate area at 3 dpw, although no defect in regenerate length, suggesting that vimentin is influencing wound healing through multiple pathways.

strengths: Larp6 knockdown produces the predicted selective effect on col1a1 but not col2a1b, consistent with Challa and Stefanovic (2011).
The partial phenocopy (area but not length defect) is logically consistent with vimentin working through multiple pathways.
Morpholino knockdown is validated by RT-PCR.
weaknesses: The regeneration data for Larp6 MO is from a single experiment in triplicate.
The partial phenocopy could indicate Larp6 is not the primary mediator of vimentin effects.
No rescue experiment is performed for Larp6.
The distinction between area and length defects is not mechanistically explained.
alternative_interpretations: Larp6 could have wound-independent effects that contribute to the area defect.
The partial phenocopy could indicate that vimentin's effects on regeneration are primarily through non-Larp6 mechanisms.
required_assumptions: Larp6 morpholino achieves specific knockdown without significant off-target effects.
The area-but-not-length defect reflects a meaningful biological distinction.
evaluation.notes: Interesting mechanistic dissection but limited replication.

nodes.label: Pharmacological inhibition of collagen cross-linking with BAPN impairs fin regen…
nodes.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of collagen cross-linking with BAPN impairs fin regeneration and disrupts SHG fiber organization at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Constant inhibition of lysyl oxidase throughout the wound healing process caused a significant reduction in regeneration of the larval fin at 2 dpw.

strengths: BAPN is a well-established lysyl oxidase inhibitor.
The fiber angle change is consistent with vimentin-deficient phenotype.
No developmental fin length defect at the concentration used.
weaknesses: BAPN causes lethality between 4-5 dpf, so experiments could only extend to 2 dpw. The authors acknowledge 'it is possible that the observed effects on regeneration were in part due to toxicity.'

The contour length actually INCREASED with BAPN treatment, which contradicts the expected direction and the vimentin MO result. The authors attribute this to measurement artifact from V-shaped fins, but this undermines the quantification approach.
BAPN affects all lysyl oxidase-dependent cross-linking, not just collagen, potentially affecting elastin and other ECM components.
Single experiment in triplicate for regeneration data.
alternative_interpretations: The regeneration defect could be due to general toxicity rather than specific collagen cross-linking inhibition.
Inhibition of elastin cross-linking or other ECM components could contribute to the phenotype.
required_assumptions: BAPN effects at the doses used are primarily through collagen cross-linking inhibition.
The observed regeneration defect is not primarily due to toxicity.
evaluation.notes: The toxicity confound significantly undermines this result. The contradictory contour length increase is also problematic.

nodes.label: Burn wounds that destroy collagen fiber integrity near the wound edge abrogate e…
nodes.claim: Burn wounds that destroy collagen fiber integrity near the wound edge abrogate epithelial projections and significantly impair regeneration compared to tail transection.
nodes.verbatim_quote: burn wounds resulting in a loss of SHG fiber integrity led to a significant reduction in the percentage of larvae displaying epithelial projections at 24 hpb.

strengths: The burn model creates a strikingly clear loss of SHG fibers near the wound edge, providing a dramatic visual comparison.
Statistically significant reduction in both projection frequency (p=0.0116) and healing area (p<0.0001).
The experiment provides a conceptually distinct test of the collagen fiber hypothesis.
Reasonable sample sizes across three replicates.
weaknesses: Burn wounds cause extensive non-specific tissue damage including cell death, protein denaturation, and altered inflammatory responses—the healing defect cannot be attributed solely to collagen loss.
Comparing burn to amputation is comparing two fundamentally different types of injury; many variables differ beyond collagen integrity.
The burn wound area measurements use individual larvae between 24-48 hours, making it unclear if this captures the full regenerative capacity.
No attempt to rescue the burn phenotype (e.g., with exogenous collagen scaffold) is made.
The different morphology of vim+ cells at the burn wound edge suggests fundamentally different wound biology, further complicating the comparison.
alternative_interpretations: The impaired healing after burn could be due to extensive cell death, altered inflammatory response, denatured growth factors, or damage to other tissue components rather than specifically collagen fiber loss.
The different vim+ cell morphology suggests the burn wound activates different repair programs, making it an inappropriate comparison for isolating collagen fiber contributions.
required_assumptions: The primary relevant difference between burn and amputation wounds is collagen fiber integrity.
Other forms of thermal damage do not significantly contribute to the healing defect.
evaluation.notes: The burn model is a creative approach but has too many confounds to specifically implicate collagen fiber loss as the cause of impaired healing.

nodes.label: The burn wound model represents a surprisingly different ECM response compared t…
nodes.claim: The burn wound model represents a surprisingly different ECM response compared to tail transection and constitutes a unique model for future studies of collagen-dependent repair.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This burn wound response was surprisingly different from the wound ECM response in the well-studied tail transection model and makes it a unique model for future studies.

strengths: The dramatic loss of SHG signal near the burn wound is indeed visually distinct from amputation.
The observation provides a basis for future investigation.
weaknesses: This is more of a future directions statement than a data-supported claim.
The 'unique model' characterization is aspirational rather than evidence-based.
Only a single comparison (burn vs. amputation) is made; no systematic characterization of the burn wound biology is performed.
Whether the burn model is practically useful depends on many factors not addressed (reproducibility, dose-response, recovery potential).
required_assumptions: The burn model is sufficiently reproducible and characterized for meaningful future studies.
The ECM differences between burn and amputation are the most relevant biological distinction.
evaluation.notes: This is essentially a discussion point/future direction rather than a testable claim with evidence.

nodes.label: Reporter activity was detected from the two somite stage, in early differentiati…
nodes.claim: Reporter activity was detected from the two somite stage, in early differentiating neurons, glial cells, cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord neurons, opercle, and developing fin mesenchymal cells at 3 dpf.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Reporter activity was detected as early as the two somite stage and later observed in early differentiating neurons in the head and in glial cells within the developing spinal cord.

strengths: Multiple panels showing expression at different stages and in different tissues.
Consistent with published in situ data from Cerdà et al. (1998).
weaknesses: Purely descriptive, qualitative data.
No quantification or systematic comparison.
required_assumptions: EGFP fluorescence accurately reports promoter activity.
evaluation.notes: Straightforward descriptive evidence.

nodes.label: Transient expression of RFP-tagged oncogenic HRasV12 from the krt4 promoter in T…
nodes.claim: Transient expression of RFP-tagged oncogenic HRasV12 from the krt4 promoter in Tg(−2vim:egfp) embryos induced EGFP in the same cells, while wild-type HRasG12 did not.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Overexpression of oncogenic HRasV12, but not wild type HRasG12, induced vimentin promoter activity and expression of EGFP that co-localized in the same cells expressing HRasV12.

strengths: Clear positive (HRasV12) and negative (HRasG12) controls.
Co-localization demonstrates cell-autonomous induction.
weaknesses: Only two replicates.
No quantification.
Transient mosaic expression provides limited sample.
required_assumptions: Two replicates are sufficient for qualitative conclusions.
evaluation.notes: Qualitative but compelling.

nodes.label: Whole mount in situ hybridization showed wound-induced vimentin RNA at the wound…
nodes.claim: Whole mount in situ hybridization showed wound-induced vimentin RNA at the wound edge at 24 hpw with the antisense but not sense probe.
nodes.verbatim_quote: we performed whole mount in situ hybridization (WMISH) to probe vimentin expression in unwounded and wounded larvae and found that tail transection induced localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hr post wound (hpw)

strengths: Sense probe negative control is appropriate.
Two experiments performed.
weaknesses: No quantification of signal.
Only 24 hpw timepoint for ISH.
required_assumptions: In situ hybridization sensitivity is sufficient to detect wound-induced changes.
evaluation.notes: Standard ISH evidence.

nodes.label: Live confocal imaging of the Tg(−2vim:egfp) reporter showed no clear signal at 2…
nodes.claim: Live confocal imaging of the Tg(−2vim:egfp) reporter showed no clear signal at 2 hpw, vim+ cells detected by 20 hpw, and enhanced expression at 26 hpw.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vim+ cells were detected by 20 hpw at the wound edge and showed enhanced expression at 26 hpw.

strengths: Live imaging provides temporal resolution of vimentin induction.
Multiple timepoints documented (2, 20, 26 hpw).
Complements ISH data.
weaknesses: Qualitative assessment; no quantification of fluorescence intensity over time.
EGFP maturation delay could shift apparent onset.
required_assumptions: EGFP maturation does not significantly delay detection relative to transcription.
evaluation.notes: Good temporal documentation of reporter induction.

nodes.label: Long-duration time-lapse confocal microscopy showed vimentin expression developi…
nodes.claim: Long-duration time-lapse confocal microscopy showed vimentin expression developing in situ at the wound edge rather than from cells migrating in.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the vim+ cells did not migrate to the wound from surrounding fin tissue but rather expression developed in what appeared to be a non-motile population of cells at the wound edge

strengths: Time-lapse imaging is the appropriate method to assess cell migration.
The zWEDGI platform enables long-term stable imaging.
weaknesses: Imaging begins at 12 hpw, missing the early post-injury window.
Temporal resolution (~12-25 min) may miss rapid migration.
No cell tracking quantification.
EGFP maturation delay could obscure early migration events.
alternative_interpretations: Cells could have migrated before 12 hpw and subsequently become non-motile.
required_assumptions: The 0-12 hpw window is not critical for cell migration to the wound edge.
EGFP-negative cells would not be migrating vim+ cells.
evaluation.notes: The technical limitations prevent definitive conclusions about migration.

nodes.label: Vim+ cells did not co-localize with krt4+ epithelial cells, did not co-localize …
nodes.claim: Vim+ cells did not co-localize with krt4+ epithelial cells, did not co-localize with a macrophage marker, and their presence was unaffected by pu.1 morpholino depletion of leukocytes.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the vim+ cells did not appear to colocalize with a macrophage marker and their presence was not influenced by the depletion of leukocytes using the pu.1 morpholino (MO)

strengths: Multiple exclusion approaches used (krt4 co-localization, mpeg1, pu.1 MO).
3D reconstructions support lack of krt4 co-localization.
weaknesses: Only negative identification (not epithelial, not macrophage); positive identity remains unknown.
pu.1 MO is a broad manipulation.
Single macrophage marker is insufficient to rule out all myeloid cells.
alternative_interpretations: The vim+ cells could be fibroblasts, pericytes, or other mesenchymal populations.
required_assumptions: The tested markers comprehensively cover the relevant cell populations.
evaluation.notes: Useful exclusion data but incomplete identification.

nodes.label: DPI treatment (1 hr pre/post wounding) reduced the ratio of vim:egfp intensity a…
nodes.claim: DPI treatment (1 hr pre/post wounding) reduced the ratio of vim:egfp intensity at the wound edge over background at 24 hpw (p=0.0282; n=12 total fins over three replicates).
nodes.verbatim_quote: Reduced reporter activity after tail transection with early ROS inhibition was quantified by assessing the relative fluorescence intensity above background at the wound edge.

strengths: Quantitative measurement (fluorescence ratio) with statistical test.
Three replicates.
weaknesses: Small total sample (n=12 fins, 2-6 per treatment per replicate).
p=0.0282 is significant but not robust.
Ratio-based quantification may be sensitive to imaging conditions.
required_assumptions: Fluorescence ratio is a valid quantification of reporter activity.
evaluation.notes: Modest but adequate quantification.

nodes.label: Morpholino depletion of Duox1 similarly reduced EGFP signal at the wound edge at…
nodes.claim: Morpholino depletion of Duox1 similarly reduced EGFP signal at the wound edge at 24 hpw.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Similar results were observed with morpholino depletion of Duox1, which is necessary for the generation of wound-induced ROS.

strengths: Genetic approach complements pharmacological (DPI) data.
Consistent with the DPI result.
weaknesses: Described qualitatively ('similar results were observed') without quantification in main text.
Presented only in supplementary figure.
Morpholino knockdown of Duox1 could have off-target effects.
required_assumptions: Duox1 MO specifically reduces wound-induced ROS.
evaluation.notes: Supportive but incompletely documented.

nodes.label: Withaferin A treatment blocked EGFP expression at 1 dpw in the reporter line, bu…
nodes.claim: Withaferin A treatment blocked EGFP expression at 1 dpw in the reporter line, but WA may also directly affect vimentin protein function.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Using a pharmacological inhibitor of NFκB activation, Withaferin A (WA)...we found that early inhibition of NFκB was sufficient to block EGFP expression at 1 dpw in the Tg(−2vim:egfp) line.

strengths: The result is consistent with NFκB involvement.
weaknesses: WA directly inhibits vimentin protein, creating an unresolvable confound for this experiment.
No quantification of the WA effect on reporter expression is provided.
No genetic NFκB manipulation is used.
Only shown in supplementary figure.
alternative_interpretations: WA could block reporter signal through direct vimentin destabilization rather than NFκB inhibition.
required_assumptions: WA effects on the reporter are primarily through NFκB rather than direct vimentin effects.
evaluation.notes: The dual activity of WA makes this evidence essentially uninterpretable for the NFκB-specific claim.

nodes.label: SHG imaging in the Tg(−2vim:egfp) line showed tight association of vim+ cells wi…
nodes.claim: SHG imaging in the Tg(−2vim:egfp) line showed tight association of vim+ cells with SHG fibers in unwounded fins, and elongated vim+ cells on intact fibers versus rounded cells near misaligned fibers in wounded fins.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We observed a tight association between the vim+ cells and the SHG fibers in unwounded caudal fins.

strengths: Direct visualization with dual-channel imaging.
3D reconstruction in both unwounded and wounded conditions.
Morphological correlation between cell shape and fiber alignment is clearly shown.
Supplementary videos provide dynamic context.
weaknesses: Qualitative observation without formal quantification of co-localization.
Only two replicates for wounded condition (24 larvae).
Correlative, not causal.
alternative_interpretations: Cells may simply respond to the mechanical environment of aligned vs. misaligned fibers.
required_assumptions: The spatial association is biologically meaningful.
evaluation.notes: Compelling imaging data, well-presented.

nodes.label: Vim MO1 reduced regenerate area at 3 dpw (p<0.0001; n=85 per treatment over four…
nodes.claim: Vim MO1 reduced regenerate area at 3 dpw (p<0.0001; n=85 per treatment over four replicates).
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae had impaired regenerate area and regenerate length at 3 dpw

strengths: Large sample size (n=85 per group).
Four replicate experiments.
Non-overlapping 95% CIs.
weaknesses: Morpholino efficacy at 3 dpw not verified at protein level.
required_assumptions: MO knockdown persists through assessment period.
evaluation.notes: Robust quantitative result.

nodes.label: F0 mosaic CRISPR mutants showed reduced regenerate area at 3 dpw (p<0.0001; ctl …
nodes.claim: F0 mosaic CRISPR mutants showed reduced regenerate area at 3 dpw (p<0.0001; ctl n=130, Vim n=119 over 3 replicates). CRISPR was validated by TOPO cloning/sequencing showing a 7 bp deletion and early stop codon.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The mosaic F0 mutants also displayed reduced regenerate length and area at 3 dpw

strengths: Large sample sizes (n=119-130).
Three replicates.
CRISPR validated by sequencing.
weaknesses: F0 mosaics have inherently variable mutational burden.
Only one sequencing example shown in detail.
The slight developmental fin area increase in CRISPR mutants is unexplained.
required_assumptions: F0 mosaics have sufficient null allele penetrance.
evaluation.notes: Good confirmatory data despite inherent F0 mosaic limitations.

nodes.label: Unwounded vim morphants showed no defect in fin length or area at 5 dpf, and TUN…
nodes.claim: Unwounded vim morphants showed no defect in fin length or area at 5 dpf, and TUNEL staining showed no apoptosis defect at 1 hpw.
